newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ business confidence turns negative - Nat. Bank.
newsitem.headline: NZ business confidence turns negative - Nat. Bank.

text.p: New Zealand business confidence has swung negative, according to the National Bank of New Zealand's monthly survey published on Monday.
Excluding last year's pre-election nerves, confidence in April was at its lowest in six years, the LLoyds TSB -owned bank said.
A net 6 percent of respondents now anticipate general business conditions to deteriorate over the next year against a net 6 percent in March who believed the economy would improve.
The fall is reflected in lower profit, investment and employment expectations.
Confience is down in all sectors, but manufacturing has taken the biggest hit and is now the most pessimistic sector.
While export volumes rose over 1996, profitability remained weak and that is reflected in low confidence in the agricultural sector, the bank said.
Chief economist Adrian Orr said monetary conditions had clearly been too tight over the past month even in comparison to what the Reserve Bank wanted.

Since the survey was conducted, March quarter inflation data had came out lower than market expectations and Orr said that that should be the catalyst for lower interest and exchange rates over coming months.

The export sector was the most wary about its economic prospects, but remains positive with a net 21 percent expecting their own activity to improve over the next year (down from 30 percent in March).
The service sector is the most optimistic with a net 30 percent expecting an improvement. Least confident is the construction sector, with only a net 2 percent expecting improvement.
Investment intentions fell across most sectors but remain positive. A net 11 percent, down from 13 percent, expect to increase investment and a net 25 percent expect to increase exports.

Inflation expectations remain stuck at around 2.7 percent annually. However, short-term pricing intentions have dropped back towards their lows. A net 9 percent plan to raise prices over the next three months.
Despite lower business confidence and pricing intentions, respondents have sharply revised up interest rate expectations.
A net 26 percent expect interest rates to rise over the next quarter, while expectations were roughly neutral last month.
